text.en: Meena saw a forest, a desert and a pond in a book. "All life, but so different," she said.

The biosphere includes all life on Earth and the parts of the land, water and atmosphere where life is found. It includes plants, animals and microbes. Ecosystems are communities of living things and their surroundings, linked by food chains and food webs.
Major biomes include forests, grasslands, deserts and tundra, each with its own climate and life. Forests, grasslands and deserts provide different habitats. Species have features that can help them survive under the conditions of each biome.
Biodiversity, the variety of life, is under threat from forest loss and pollution. Protected areas such as national parks and biosphere reserves, for example the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, help conserve it.

Forests, grasslands and deserts provide different habitats. Species have features that can help them survive under the conditions of each biome.
Biodiversity, the variety of life, is under threat from forest loss and pollution.
Protected areas such as national parks and biosphere reserves, for example the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, help conserve it.
A pond, a field and a forest each contain living things and nonliving surroundings. We can study each as an ecosystem by examining the interactions within it.
Biotic components are the living parts, such as plants and animals. Abiotic components include light, water, air, soil and temperature.
An ecosystem can be small, such as a pond, or larger, such as a forest region. A boundary can help us ask a focused question, even though energy and matter cross it.

board.text: An ecosystem boundary depends on the question

text.en: Green plants use light energy to make sugars. We call them producers because they produce organic material that can enter a food chain.
A grasshopper feeding on leaves is a primary consumer. An insect-eating bird can act as a secondary consumer. Name each role from what the organism eats in the example.
Some fungi and bacteria help break down dead organic material. This can return nutrients to the surroundings where they can be taken up again.
An arrow in a food-chain diagram shows a transfer from food to consumer. An arrow from grass to rabbit means that the rabbit obtains energy by feeding on grass.
A food web combines more than one chain. A hawk may feed on more than one kind of animal. Trace each path separately to see where the links overlap.

board.text: A food web shows connected feeding paths

text.en: Some energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat at every feeding level. Less energy is available to organisms at higher levels. Matter can be recycled while energy flows through the system.
If one population changes, a food web can help us predict possible effects. The real outcome also depends on other foods, habitats and the strength of the connections.

board.text: A diagram supports a prediction, not certainty

text.en: Biodiversity can refer to differences within a species, the number and kinds of species, or the variety of ecosystems. A forest may show all three kinds of diversity.
Habitat loss can reduce the places where a species feeds or breeds. Fragmentation can separate the remaining patches, making movement harder for some species.

board.text: Habitat loss and fragmentation affect species differently

text.en: Pollution, overuse of resources and changing climate can also affect biodiversity. Which change matters most depends on the species and place being studied.

board.text: Check the local evidence before identifying a cause

text.en: A biome is a broad region with characteristic climate and life. Climate influences the kinds of plants that grow well, while soils, fire and land use can also play a role.

board.text: Biome: broad climate and life pattern

text.en: Warm wet tropical forests often support many species. Coniferous forests are characteristic of large areas with cold seasons. Compare temperature and rainfall before deciding how a forest fits a biome.
Grasslands often have extensive grasses and relatively few trees. Savannas can have scattered trees, while other grasslands may have few. Seasonal water supply can shape both.

board.text: Grasslands include more than one type

text.en: Deserts have low precipitation. Some are hot and others are cold. Tundra is generally cold with a short growing season. Compare both temperature and moisture.

board.text: Desert: low precipitation · tundra: cold, short season

text.en: Aquatic biomes include freshwater and marine settings. A lake, an estuary and the open sea differ in salt content and often in depth, movement and light.

board.text: Aquatic settings differ in salinity and other conditions

text.en: An estuary is a coastal setting where fresh and salt water can mix. Its conditions can change with tides and river flow, affecting which organisms can live there.

Protected habitats can conserve species where they live. The Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve is a local example from the chapter. Conservation also involves cooperation with people who live and work nearby.

board.text: Conservation can protect habitats in place

text.en: Conservation outside a natural habitat can include a botanical garden or a seed bank. It can support some goals, while protecting living habitats serves other needs.

board.text: In-place and outside-habitat conservation have different roles

text.en: Choose two parts of a food web and explain their relationship. Then name one nonliving factor or habitat change that may affect that connection.

board.text: Link feeding relationships with habitat conditions

text.en: Compare two ecosystems using the same criteria: water availability, particular living groups and one interaction. State which observation is evidence for each comparison.

problem.en: Grass is eaten by a grasshopper, and an insect-eating bird eats that grasshopper. Identify the roles and read the arrows.

text.en: Put grass at the start of the chain.

why.en: It is the producer and makes sugars using light energy.

text.en: Follow arrows from grass to grasshopper to bird.

why.en: The first consumer eats the producer. The second eats the first consumer.
